summary: YANG is a data modeling language for configuration data, state data, remote procedure calls and notifications used by network management protocols. This proposed standard describes the syntax and semantics of version 1.1, a maintenance release that fixes ambiguities and defects in the original.

eli5.summary: YANG is like a form template for a network device that lists every setting and meter, what kind of answer each needs, and how they relate. Version 1.1 fixes confusing spots in the first version.

subtitle: The language network engineers use to describe, as a typed tree, every setting, meter, operation and alert a managed device exposes.

tldr.problem: Network management protocols such as NETCONF need a precise, machine-readable way to describe configuration data, state data, remote procedure calls and notifications, so that clients and servers agree on what the data means.
tldr.mechanism: YANG organizes data as a tree of modules containing leaf, leaf-list, container and list nodes with typed values and constraints. Groupings, augments, features and deviations let models be reused, extended and honestly adapted. Version 1.1 also defines how this data is encoded in XML and manipulated with NETCONF.
tldr.outcome: YANG 1.1 is a maintenance release of the original YANG that fixes ambiguities and defects, with a small number of backward incompatibilities. It is a Proposed Standard, does not obsolete RFC 6020, and has since been updated by RFC 8342 and RFC 8526.

today: RFC 7950 is a Proposed Standard that does not obsolete RFC 6020, and it has been updated by RFC 8342 and RFC 8526.

sections.title: What YANG Is For
sections.content:
YANG is a data modeling language. It was originally designed to model the configuration and state data manipulated by the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF), plus NETCONF remote procedure calls and notifications. Since version 1 appeared in RFC 6020, YANG has also been used or proposed for other protocols, and encodings other than XML have been proposed, such as JSON in RFC 7951.

This document specifies the syntax and semantics of version 1.1 of the language. It also says how data defined by a YANG module is encoded in XML and how NETCONF operations manipulate it. Other protocols and encodings are explicitly out of scope. The RFC states that it does not obsolete RFC 6020.

YANG 1.1 is a maintenance release, addressing ambiguities and defects in the original. A small number of changes are not backward compatible: the escape rules inside double-quoted strings changed, unquoted strings cannot contain quote characters, when and if-feature are illegal on list keys, the legal characters in a module are now defined, and noncharacters are illegal in the string type.

New in 1.1 are, among others, the action statement, notifications tied to data nodes, the anydata statement, boolean expressions in if-feature, leaf-lists with default values, and several new XPath functions.
sections.eli5: Imagine every toaster, fridge and oven in a building came with a different manual. YANG is a single, strict way to write the manual so a computer can read it. Version 1.1 cleans up places where the first version was confusing.

sections.title: The Four Kinds of Data Nodes
sections.content:
YANG models data as a tree in which each node has a name and either a value or a set of child nodes. Four node kinds do most of the work.

  • A leaf holds one value of a particular type and has no children, for example a host name.
  • A leaf-list is a sequence of values of one type, such as a list of domain names to search.
  • A container groups related nodes in a subtree. It has no value of its own.
  • A list defines a sequence of entries, each like a container. Entries are uniquely identified by the values of the list's key leafs.

Containers come in two styles. A non-presence container exists only to organize the hierarchy, so an empty one means the same as an absent one. A presence container, marked with the presence statement, means something by existing: in the RFC's example, an ssh container whose presence enables SSH.

A choice contains case branches that cannot appear together. Choice and case nodes exist only in the schema tree, not in the data tree. Creating a node from one case implicitly deletes nodes from every other case.

The RFC's running example puts a host-name leaf, a domain-search leaf-list and a login container with a user list into one module called example-system.
sections.eli5: Think of a filing cabinet. A leaf is one sticky note with one answer on it. A container is a labelled folder. A list is a stack of identical forms, each with its own name at the top. A choice is a menu where you may pick only one meal.

sections.title: Modules, Submodules and Imports
sections.content:
The module is the base unit of definition. A module defines a single data model, or augments an existing one. A module header carries yang-version, namespace and prefix, followed by imports, includes, meta-information such as organization and contact, revision history, and then the definitions. Module names must be unique within a server, and the RFC recommends names unlikely to collide with others, for example by using an organization name as a prefix.

A submodule is a partial module. A module may include any number of submodules but each submodule belongs to only one module, and the outside world still sees a single module. In YANG 1.1 a submodule can reference definitions in all submodules of its module without using include.

The import statement makes another module's definitions available under a local prefix, written as prefix:name. An import may name a specific revision-date, which protects the importing module when the imported one evolves. If no revision is given, it is undefined which revision is used. There must be no circular chains of imports.

Each module is bound to a distinct XML namespace, which is a globally unique URI. YANG itself defines the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:1 for NETCONF edit-config operations, error-info content and the action element. Files are typically named after the module, with the extension .yang for YANG syntax or .yin for YIN syntax.

Names of groupings, types and identities are resolved where they are defined, not where they are used, like static scoping in a programming language. Typedefs and groupings can be nested to keep them private to a module or submodule.
sections.eli5: A module is like a recipe book with its own name and cover. It can borrow a recipe from another book, but must say which book and which edition, so nothing changes under it by surprise.

sections.title: Configuration, State and Built-In Types
sections.content:
YANG separates settings from measurements with the config statement. A node tagged config true is configuration, which lives in configuration datastores. A node tagged config false is state data, which does not. If config is not given, a node inherits its parent's value, and the top default is true. Nothing under a config false node can be config true. In the RFC's interface example, a speed leaf is configured while an observed-speed leaf is state.

Every leaf has a type. YANG has a set of built-in types, listed below. New types are derived with typedef and can restrict a base type with a range, length or pattern. The RFC's example is a percent type that is a uint8 restricted to the range 0 .. 100.

Some types are worth a closer look. A decimal64 must give a fraction-digits value from 1 to 18. A leafref points at another leaf through a path and by default requires that the referenced instance exist. An identityref refers to an identity, and valid values are those derived from all its base identities. An enumeration or bits type can be subtyped in 1.1.

Values are conceptually stored in canonical form, and a server sending XML must use the canonical form. A default value applies when the leaf is absent, subject to its ancestors and any when or if-feature condition.
sections.eli5: Some boxes on the form are things you write in, like a thermostat setting. Others are gauges you can only read, like the room temperature. Each box also says what kind of answer fits, such as a whole number from 0 to 100.

sections.title: Syntax, XPath and YIN
sections.content:
YANG syntax is C-like, chosen for readability, since YANG values the time of readers of models over that of module writers and tool developers. Every statement is a keyword, zero or one argument, and either a semicolon or a block in braces. Comments are C++ style. Modules are stored as UTF-8. Strings can be unquoted, single-quoted (every character preserved) or double-quoted (backslash escapes are limited to newline, tab, double quote and backslash). Quoted strings can be joined with +. Identifiers are case sensitive, and implementations MUST support identifiers of up to 64 characters.

Many references and dependencies use XML Path Language (XPath) 1.0 as notation. An implementation does not have to contain an XPath interpreter, but it MUST enforce the requirements the model encodes. The data tree has no document order, so expressions SHOULD NOT depend on one. XPath numbers are double-precision floating point, so some 64-bit values cannot be represented exactly and equality comparisons on them can give unexpected results.

Section 10 adds XPath functions: current(), re-match(), deref(), derived-from(), derived-from-or-self(), enum-value() and bit-is-set().

YIN is an XML form of the same information. The mapping from YANG to YIN is semantically lossless, with one YIN element per YANG keyword, so XML tools such as XSLT can work on models. Comments and whitespace are not preserved. YIN elements live in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:yin:1. The full YANG grammar is given in ABNF in Section 14.
sections.eli5: YANG is written so people can read it easily, like a tidy recipe card with brackets for each step. YIN is the same recipe typed in another alphabet that other computer tools like better.

sections.title: Reuse and Extension
sections.content:
A grouping is a reusable set of schema nodes. It defines nothing by itself; a uses statement instantiates it, and refine can tailor it, for example by replacing a description, adding a default, or changing mandatory or min-elements. The RFC shows one target grouping (an address and a port) used for both the source and the destination of a connection.

The augment statement adds nodes to a schema tree defined elsewhere, including in another module, which the RFC says is useful for vendors adding vendor-specific parameters to standard models in an interoperable way. The augmenting module's namespace qualifies the added XML elements. If an augment adds mandatory configuration nodes to another module's node, it MUST be made conditional with when so that clients that do not know the augmenting module do not break.

An identity is a globally unique, abstract, untyped name that may be derived from one or more base identities. Together with identityref this gives an extensible set of named values. Finally, the extension statement lets standards bodies, vendors and individuals define new statements that attach non-YANG semantics, and the syntax makes them stand out from standard ones.
sections.eli5: A grouping is a cookie cutter you can press out again and again. An augment is like adding an extra page to someone else's notebook without tearing it. An extension lets you invent a new kind of sticker for your own pages.

sections.title: Operations and Notifications
sections.content:
YANG can describe things a device does, not just what it stores. An rpc defines a top-level operation with an optional input and output, whose parameters are modeled with ordinary data definition statements. The RFC's example is activate-software-image, with an image-name input and a status output, carried in a NETCONF rpc and rpc-reply.

Version 1.1 adds action, an operation tied to a specific container or list node. The RFC states the difference plainly: an action is tied to a node in the datastore, whereas an rpc is not, so invoking an action names the node along with the action and its input. An action cannot be defined inside an rpc, another action or a notification, and cannot sit under a list that has no key.

A notification defines an event message, with its content modeled by data definition statements. In 1.1 a notification can be defined at the top level of a module or attached to a container or list node. The RFC's example is a link-failure notification carrying an interface name and its administrative and operational status.

Because input and notification trees are not part of any datastore, config statements inside them are ignored. Mandatory leafs must be present, and defaults apply as they do for leafs elsewhere.
sections.eli5: Besides dials and gauges, a machine can have buttons and alarms. An rpc is a button on the control panel. An action is a button that belongs to one particular machine. A notification is the alarm bell that rings when something happens.

sections.title: Constraints, Features and Deviations
sections.content:
YANG models can state rules that valid data must obey. Leaf values must match their type restrictions, all list keys must be present, at most one case of a choice may have nodes, and a must statement holds an XPath expression that MUST evaluate to true. Other constraints are unique for lists, min-elements and max-elements, mandatory, and referential integrity through leafref paths. The running configuration datastore MUST always be valid. For NETCONF, constraints are enforced while parsing payloads, while processing edit-config, and at validation time. For the candidate datastore, validation waits for a commit or validate operation.

Section 15 defines the NETCONF errors for violations. A broken unique returns operation-failed with the app tag data-not-unique, and a broken must returns the app tag must-violation, unless the statement supplies its own error-app-tag.

Conformance, meaning how faithfully a server follows a model, has three mechanisms. The basic behavior of the model is a contract between client and server. A feature marks parts of the model as optional, and if-feature ties definitions to it; the 1.1 argument is a boolean expression over feature names. A deviation lets a server declare how it fails to implement part of a module, using deviate with not-supported, add, replace or delete. The RFC says deviations are strongly discouraged, are a last resort, and must never be part of a published standard.

A NETCONF server announces its modules through the ietf-yang-library module from RFC 7895. It must also advertise a yang-library capability in its hello message carrying a module-set-id, so a client can cache the module list until that value changes. A server must not implement more than one revision of a module.
sections.eli5: A good form refuses wrong answers, like a birthday box that will not accept the number 99 for the month. Features are extras that only some machines have, like a toaster with a bagel setting. A deviation is a machine admitting honestly, I cannot do that part.

sections.title: Updating Modules and Living with Version 1
sections.content:
Published modules have to evolve without breaking clients written against earlier versions. Every published change needs a new revision statement at the front of the list. The module name and the namespace must never change, and obsolete definitions must not be removed. Allowed changes include adding enums or bits (without changing existing values), expanding a range, length or pattern, adding a default to a leaf that has none, relaxing a must or when, moving status from current to deprecated to obsolete, and adding new typedefs, groupings, features and identities. Anything that changes the meaning of an old definition must be a new definition with a new identifier.

Version 1 and version 1.1 modules can coexist, within limits. A 1.1 module must not include a version 1 submodule, and the reverse is also forbidden. A version 1 module must not import a 1.1 module by revision, while a 1.1 module may import a version 1 module by revision. The RFC explains that this avoids a cascade in which updating one module to 1.1 forces every module that imports it to be updated too. A module with no yang-version statement, or with the value 1, is a YANG version 1 module as defined in RFC 6020, while 1.1 modules MUST say 1.1.

One change to NETCONF advertising is also worth knowing: a server advertises support for YANG 1.1 modules through ietf-yang-library rather than listing them as capabilities in the hello message.
sections.eli5: If you change the rules of a game after everyone has the old rulebook, people get confused. So YANG only lets you make changes that never turn a move that used to be legal into an illegal one. Anything bigger needs a brand-new game name.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the language itself has no security impact on the Internet. Security concerns come from how data modeled in YANG is used: the same considerations apply as for the base NETCONF protocol in RFC 6241. Modeled data and the RPCs and notifications defined in YANG may carry sensitive information, so it depends on the security of the transmission infrastructure, the security of the applications that store or release it, and adequate authentication and access control. Such issues are to be handled by the documents that define each data model and the interfaces used to manipulate it.

The RFC adds a warning for tool authors: YANG parsers need to be robust against malformed documents. Reading malformed documents from unknown or untrusted sources could let an attacker gain the privileges of the user running the parser and, in an extreme case, compromise the whole machine.

The only IANA action is the registration of one NETCONF capability identifier, :yang-library, with the URN urn:ietf:params:netconf:capability:yang-library:1.0.
sections.eli5: A rulebook for describing machines is not dangerous by itself. But the secrets inside the machines still need locks, and any program that reads these rulebooks must be careful with sneaky, broken ones.
